blocks.content: docker rm permanently deletes a container, its writable layer and all. Unlike stopping, this cannot be undone by simply starting it again, the container is genuinely gone.

Removing a container deletes its writable layer, along with any files that lived only there and were never persisted to a volume. Once removed, there is no docker start that can bring that specific container back, its identity and writable state are gone for good.

blocks.alt: The writable layer, and everything only stored there, is gone

blocks.content:
docker rm web
# Deletes the stopped container "web" permanently.

code.content:
docker rm web
# Deletes the stopped container "web" permanently.

codes.bash:

# Deletes the stopped container "web" permanently.

blocks.content: 2. A Running Container Must Be Stopped First
blocks.text: 2. A Running Container Must Be Stopped First

blocks.content: By default, docker rm refuses to remove a container that is still running, you have to stop it first. The -f (force) flag skips that safety check, stopping and removing in one step, useful in scripts but worth using deliberately, not by habit.

blocks.alt: A running container needs -f, a stopped one does not

blocks.content:
docker rm web            # fails if "web" is still running
docker rm -f web         # stops it (hard) and removes it in one step

code.content:
docker rm web            # fails if "web" is still running
docker rm -f web         # stops it (hard) and removes it in one step

codes.bash:
docker rm web            # fails if "web" is still running
docker rm -f web         # stops it (hard) and removes it in one step

blocks.content: Removing a container has zero effect on the image it was created from. The image is a separate, shared, read-only artifact, removing every container ever started from it does not remove the image itself, that is what docker rmi is for.

blocks.alt: The image survives every container built from it

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker rm permanently deletes a container's writable layer, this is not reversible the way stopping is.
Removing containers never touches the underlying image, images and containers are removed with entirely separate commands.
